passages.t: A man from Saul's camp, with a crown
passages.happening:
Second Samuel begins where 1 Samuel ended. ‘After the death of Saul, David returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag two days’ (verse 1).

On the third day a man arrives from Saul's camp ‘with torn clothes and dust on his head’ (verse 2), and he falls to the ground before David. “Where have you come from?” David asked. “I have escaped from the Israelite camp,” he replied (verse 3).

He tells David that the army has fled, that many have fallen, and that Saul and Jonathan are dead. David asks how he knows. The man says that he happened to be on Mount Gilboa, that he found Saul wounded with the enemy closing in, that Saul begged him to kill him, and that he did. ‘And I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
David is at Ziklag, the town in the western Negev that Achish of Gath had given him (1 Samuel 27:6). He has just come back from defeating the Amalekites who raided it. Far to the north, the Philistines have won on Mount Gilboa. It is about 1010 BC. Israel has no king, no army in the field and no clear heir, since three of Saul's sons died with him.

Torn clothes and dust on the head were the signs of grief and of bad news. The man arrives dressed as a mourner, perhaps sincerely, perhaps to play the part. And he brings Saul's crown and the band from his arm, the signs of a king. To lay them before David was a way of saying that he was the new king, and that the bearer deserved thanks for it.

A first hearer would notice two things about him. He is an Amalekite, one of the people David has just been fighting. And his story does not match the one 1 Samuel 31 told, where Saul, badly wounded, took his own life, and his armor-bearer died with him. Most readers conclude that this man found Saul's body on the battlefield, took the crown and the armband, and made up the rest to win a reward from the man he expected to be king. ‘I happened to be on Mount Gilboa’ (verse 6) is a suspicious way to begin.
passages.later:
Chronicles tells the end of Saul as 1 Samuel 31 does, with no Amalekite in it (1 Chronicles 10:1-6), and it adds its own verdict on his reign: ‘So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD’ (1 Chronicles 10:13).

There is a bitter irony in who brings the crown. Saul's kingdom had been taken from him over Amalek. At Endor he heard that it was torn from him and given to David, ‘Because you did not obey the LORD or carry out His burning anger against Amalek’ (1 Samuel 28:18). Now an Amalekite carries Saul's crown to David.
passages.hard:
Two accounts of Saul's death. Which is true?

The narrator of 1 Samuel 31 says that Saul, wounded and afraid of being taken alive, took his own life. This man says that he killed Saul at Saul's own request. Most interpreters believe the man was lying, hoping for a reward. A few suggest that the two accounts come from separate traditions, or that Saul was still alive when the man found him.

Either way, the chapter makes one thing plain. David judges the man by his own words. He came claiming to have killed the LORD's anointed, and that claim is what condemns him.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The man thought he knew what a rising king would want to hear. Ask whether you have ever tried to win someone's favor by bringing them news of a rival's fall. And ask what it would take to tell the truth when a lie looks like it will be rewarded.

passages.t: David mourns, and judges the messenger
passages.happening:
David does not take the crown and celebrate. ‘Then David took hold of his own clothes and tore them, and all the men who were with him did the same’ (verse 11). They mourn, weep and fast until evening for Saul and Jonathan, ‘and for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword’ (verse 12).

Then David questions the messenger again. The man says he is ‘the son of a foreigner’, an Amalekite (verse 13). “Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” (verse 14). David orders one of his young men to strike him down, and he dies. David's last words to him are the verdict: “Your blood be on your own head because your own mouth has testified against you” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Tearing one's clothes, weeping and fasting until evening were the ordinary signs of grief in Israel. What is not ordinary is the man David grieves for. For years Saul had hunted him. Now Saul is dead and the throne is open, and David mourns him with all his men.

‘The son of a foreigner’ is the word for a resident alien, a foreigner living in Israel under its protection and its laws. That matters. The man cannot plead that he did not know what the LORD's anointed king meant to Israel.

David's question goes back to the conviction that ruled his outlaw years. Twice he had Saul in his power and would not harm him, because Saul was the LORD's anointed (1 Samuel 24 and 26). The anointed king belonged to God, and no one was to rise by shedding his blood. Now a man has come claiming exactly that, and expecting thanks.

‘Your blood be on your own head’ was a formula for guilt that falls back on the guilty person. The man's own testimony convicted him. So at the very start of the reign the chapter shows two things: David will not receive the kingdom as a prize taken from Saul's body, and no one will win his favor by shedding blood for him.
passages.later: The same words for guilt that falls back on the guilty appear elsewhere. The spies told Rahab that if anyone left her house in the attack, ‘his blood will be on his own head’ (Joshua 2:19). And when Solomon ordered Joab's death for the murders of Abner and Amasa, he said, ‘The LORD will bring his bloodshed back upon his own head’ (1 Kings 2:32).
passages.asks: David grieved honestly for a man who had wronged him for years. Ask whether there is someone who hurt you whose loss you could still grieve. And ask where you are tempted to welcome someone's fall because it clears your own way.

passages.happening:
Then David sings a lament for Saul and Jonathan. He orders that the people of Judah be taught it, the Song of the Bow, and the narrator adds, ‘It is written in the Book of Jashar’ (verse 18).

It opens, “Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen!” (verse 19). He does not want the news told in the Philistine cities of Gath and Ashkelon, where the women would rejoice (verse 20). He asks the mountains of Gilboa to have no dew or rain, because there ‘the shield of the mighty was defiled’ (verse 21).

He praises the two men as warriors: “Saul and Jonathan, beloved and delightful in life, were not divided in death. They were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions” (verse 23). He calls the women of Israel to weep for Saul, who clothed them in scarlet and gold (verse 24).

Then he turns to his friend: “I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were delightful to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women” (verse 26). The song ends where it began: “How the mighty have fallen and the weapons of war have perished!” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
A lament was a known form of song, a poem sung over the dead. The Book of Jashar was a collection of poetry that is now lost. Joshua quotes it too, so it seems to have gathered songs of Israel's early wars.

The poem is built around its refrain, ‘How the mighty have fallen’, at the opening, the middle and the close (verses 19, 25 and 27). The word for the mighty means warriors, heroes of battle. It honors Saul and Jonathan as true fighters, whatever Saul's failures, and the grief lies in the gap between their strength and their end. The first line's word for glory can also mean a gazelle, and some translators read the line as the gazelle of Israel lies slain, a picture of swift and graceful warriors.

Gath and Ashkelon were two of the five Philistine cities. Their women would celebrate the victory with songs and dances, as Israel's women once did for David (1 Samuel 18:6-7). David cannot bear to think of it.

Notice what the song leaves out. It never mentions God, and it never mentions Saul's sins. It praises Saul for his courage and for the prosperity he brought his people. It moves from Israel's grief for its king to David's own grief for his friend, and the last stanza, spoken to Jonathan himself, holds the most personal lines in the book.
passages.later:
The same kind of lament is heard in the prophets, and it fills the book of Lamentations. Micah, mourning over the towns of Judah as an invader comes near, begins with David's words turned round: ‘Do not tell it in Gath’ (Micah 1:10).

The Book of Jashar is named once more in the Bible, after the long day of Joshua's battle: ‘Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?’ (Joshua 10:13).
passages.hard:
What does David mean when he says that Jonathan's love surpassed the love of women?

Some modern readers take these words as evidence of a romantic or sexual relationship. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, read them as the language of deep covenant friendship. They note that the Hebrew word for love in this verse is used very widely, even for political loyalty: where 1 Kings says that Hiram king of Tyre ‘had always been a friend of David’ (1 Kings 5:1), the Hebrew uses this word. They note that the friendship was sealed by a covenant (1 Samuel 18:3), and that the comparison is about a loyalty that cost Jonathan his own claim to the throne. And they point out that the book describes David's sexual history elsewhere plainly, and nothing like it is described here.

Readers should know that both readings exist, and weigh them against the text itself. What no one disputes is the depth of the bond. Jonathan's love was faithful and costly, and David grieves it as the greatest human loyalty he had known.
passages.asks: David put his grief into a song and had it taught to his people. Ask whether you have let yourself grieve a loss, or hurried past it. And ask whether there is someone whose faithfulness to you deserves to be said out loud.
